questions.q: The gift-card feature worked in the demo. Why was that not enough?
questions.explain: Ada redeeming her own card worked. Five things any curious user could try all caused real incidents: injection, acting as someone else, creating money, losing money and reading other people's balances.
options: Demos always run on slower computers
The demo only tried the happy path; the internet will send wrong, hostile and parallel requests, so you must attack your own endpoints the same way
Demos do not use a database
Because the code had no comments

questions.q: What made the SQL injection in GET /giftcards?code=… possible?
questions.explain: When input becomes part of the SQL text, the input can change the query. With a $1 placeholder the value travels separately and is only ever compared as data.
options: The database had no password
The code was glued into the SQL text with a template string, so a quote in the input could end the string and add OR '1'='1'
The route used GET instead of POST
The gift card table had no primary key

questions.q: This is how the broken server built its query. What does it print?
questions.explain: The quote in the input closes the SQL string, and OR '1'='1' is true for every row. The lookup for one card became "every card", and Ada learned Linus's unused code.
options: SELECT * FROM gift_cards WHERE code = 'x' OR '1'='1'
SELECT * FROM gift_cards WHERE code = 'x\' OR \'1\'=\'1'
SELECT * FROM gift_cards WHERE code = '${code}'
SELECT * FROM gift_cards WHERE code = "x' OR '1'='1"

questions.q: The fixed code keeps the SQL text and the values apart. What does this print?
questions.explain: The SQL text never changes, whatever the input is. The database looks for a card literally named x' OR '1'='1 and finds none. Node prints a string with single quotes inside using double quotes.
options:
SELECT amount_cents FROM gift_cards WHERE code = $1
[ "x' OR '1'='1" ]

SELECT amount_cents FROM gift_cards WHERE code = 'x' OR '1'='1'
[]

SELECT amount_cents FROM gift_cards WHERE code = $1
[ 'x' OR '1'='1' ]

SELECT amount_cents FROM gift_cards WHERE code = x' OR '1'='1
[ "x' OR '1'='1" ]

questions.q: The fixed code checks every gift code against a regular expression. Does it still need the $1 placeholder?
questions.explain: Defence in depth. Even without the schema, the parameterized query would have answered 404 for the injection string instead of listing every card.
options: No, validation alone makes SQL safe
Yes: validation is one wall and parameters are the second; if a future change loosens the schema, the query is still safe
No, placeholders are only needed for numbers
Only when the database is PostgreSQL

questions.q: The fixed module accepts a gift code only if it matches this pattern. What does this print?
questions.explain: Codes are upper case, start with GIFT-, and have 4 to 40 more characters. GIFT-AB has only 2. The injection string contains quotes and spaces, so it never reaches SQL.
options: [ true, false, false, false ]
[ true, false, true, false ]
[ true, false, true, true ]
[ true, true, false, false ]

questions.q: The broken /giftcards/redeem read userId from the request body. What is the fix?
questions.explain: Anything in the request can be chosen by the caller. With identity from the body, anyone could act as anyone, with no login at all. The fixed server has no route that accepts a user id for "who am I".
options: Check that userId is a positive number
Hide the field in the browser's form
Take the user only from the session token: hash the bearer token and look up the hash; ignore any user id in the body
Encrypt the userId before sending it

questions.q: GET /wallets/:userId let anyone read anyone's balance. What is this kind of bug called?
questions.explain: Changing a number in the URL was enough to see another user's data. The fix is /wallets/me: the wallet is found from the caller's session, never from the URL.
options: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
An IDOR, an insecure direct object reference: nothing checks that the object belongs to the caller
A race condition
A denial of service

questions.q: Ada "sent" Linus -3000 cents. The first UPDATE added 30.00 to Ada, the second failed on the CHECK and answered 500. Which two missing things caused the damage?
questions.explain: Validation would have refused the negative amount with 400. A transaction would have rolled back the first write when the second failed. With neither, money was created.
options: A rate limit and a cache
Input validation (amounts must be 1 to 100000 cents) and a transaction around the two writes
HTTPS and a stronger password
A bigger connection pool and a timeout

questions.q: This copies the broken transfer: two separate writes, no validation, no transaction. What does it print?
questions.explain: Taking -3000 from Ada adds 3000. The second write would make Linus negative, so the CHECK fails and the answer is 500, but the first write already happened. Ada gained 30.00 out of nothing.

questions.q: Linus sent 1000 cents to user 99, who does not exist, and got 200. What check was missing?
questions.explain: An UPDATE that matches no row is not an error for the database. The fix checks affectedRows after each UPDATE and throws when it is 0, which rolls back the whole transaction.
options: A check of Linus's password
A check of the write's result: the credit UPDATE matched 0 rows, and nobody looked at affectedRows
A check that 1000 is an even number
A check of the Content-Type header

questions.q: This transfer runs inside a fake transaction that throws away the changes on error. What does it print?
questions.explain: The debit happened only on the draft. The missing receiver threw, the draft was thrown away, and Linus still has 10.00. That is what db.transaction does with ROLLBACK.

questions.q: Two redemptions of the same card arrive at the same moment. Why did the broken code pay twice?
questions.explain: Between reading and writing there is a gap, and another request can run in it. The fix removes the gap.
options: Because the card code was too short
Both requests ran the SELECT, both saw "not redeemed", and both credited the wallet before either marked the card: a check-then-act race
Because PostgreSQL runs every query twice
Because the HTTP server retried the request

questions.q: Which statement claims a gift card safely, even under parallel requests?
questions.explain: One statement checks and claims the card. The second request finds redeemed_by already set, matches no row and gets 404. It is the same idea as ShopFlow's conditional stock UPDATE.
options: SELECT * FROM gift_cards WHERE code = $1, then UPDATE gift_cards SET redeemed_by = $2 WHERE code = $1
UPDATE gift_cards SET redeemed_by = $1 WHERE code = $2 AND redeemed_by IS NULL RETURNING amount_cents
UPDATE gift_cards SET redeemed_by = $1 WHERE code = $2
DELETE FROM gift_cards WHERE code = $1 after crediting the wallet

questions.q: This copies the broken "SELECT, then UPDATE" redemption. Two requests run at the same time. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both requests read "unused" before either wrote. Both credited 50.00, so a 50.00 card paid 100.00. Awaiting anything between the check and the write opens this gap.

questions.q: Now the check and the claim happen in one step, like UPDATE … AND redeemed_by IS NULL. What does this print?
questions.explain: The first request claims the card. The second finds it already claimed and gets 404. The card pays once: 10.00 + 50.00 = 60.00, like the lesson's test with Promise.allSettled.

questions.q: The fixed module parses transfers with this schema. What does it print?
questions.explain: Amounts are whole cents from 1 to 100000. Negative, zero, fractional and huge amounts are refused with 400 before any SQL runs.
options: [ false, false, false, true, false ]
[ false, true, true, true, false ]
[ false, false, true, true, true ]
[ true, false, false, true, false ]

questions.q: Why does the fixed transfer throw a ValidationError when to equals the caller's own id?
questions.explain: Business rules live in the module, next to the schema. A clear 400 is better than an operation that does nothing useful and still shows up in the audit trail.
options: Because the database cannot update the same row twice
Sending money to yourself has no business meaning, so the rule refuses it instead of producing confusing ledger entries
Because it would always create money
Because the schema cannot compare two fields

questions.q: What is wrong with returning SELECT * results to the client?
questions.explain: Name the columns you want to show. The fixed card returns only amountCents and a redeemed flag.
options: It is slower than naming columns
It sends internal columns, such as redeemed_by user ids, to anyone who asks, and any new column leaks automatically
It returns the rows in random order
PostgreSQL does not allow it

questions.q: The fixed lookup shows a card without internal columns. What does this print?
questions.explain: The client learns what it needs, the amount and whether the card is used, but not who used it. That is the SQL version redeemed_by IS NOT NULL AS redeemed in JavaScript.
options: { amountCents: 2000, redeemed: true }
{ code: 'GIFT-LINUS-2000', amount_cents: 2000, redeemed_by: 2 }
{ amountCents: 2000, redeemed: 2 }
{ amountCents: 2000, redeemed: false }

questions.q: Why does the fix move the rules into a wallets.ts module with no HTTP in it?
questions.explain: The HTTP layer only reads, authenticates and delegates. The tests call wallets.redeem and wallets.transfer directly, with a fresh database each time.
options: Because HTTP handlers cannot use SQL
Rules mixed into route handlers cannot be tested or reused without HTTP; a module can be tested directly and the HTTP layer stays thin
Because modules run faster than route handlers
So the module can read the user id from the body

questions.q: The fixed server finds the user from the bearer token only. What does this print?
questions.explain: The body says userId: 1, but the token belongs to Linus, so the caller is user 2. The body's user id is simply ignored. No token means 401.
options:
user 2
401 Log in first

user 1
401 Log in first

user 2
user 1

401 Log in first
401 Log in first

questions.q: The fixed module throws errors from @zudojs/errors. What status does each one become?
questions.explain: Each error carries its own status, and @zudojs/http turns it into a JSON answer. A bad request gets 400, never 500.

questions.q: After the fixed server survived the attacks, the lesson checks that "the money adds up". What does this print?
questions.explain: Wallets plus unused cards must stay the same: Ada's card moved 50.00 into her wallet, and Linus's card is still unused. With the broken code the same check would show money created.
options: 9000 9000 adds up
9000 7000 money created or lost
2000 7000 money created or lost
9000 11000 money created or lost

questions.q: Why must gift-code lookups and redemptions be rate-limited?
questions.explain: Codes are secrets that are worth money. Limit per user and per IP, and count failed redemptions per user.
options: To save database space
Without a limit, an attacker can guess codes by brute force; ten wrong codes in a row should lock redemption for 15 minutes
Because gift codes expire after 15 minutes
So that the cache has time to fill

questions.q: Should wallet balances be cached?
questions.explain: A cached balance could be out of date and let someone spend money twice or see the wrong amount. Caching card lookups would mostly help attackers guessing codes.
options: Yes, for 60 seconds, to make the page faster
No: they must always be exact, and the query is a primary-key lookup that is already fast
Yes, but only for admins
Yes, forever, and clear the cache on every deploy

questions.q: What should the request logs of the wallet service contain?
questions.explain: A gift code in a log is money anyone with log access can spend. The logger's redaction does not know that code is secret here, so leave it out yourself.
options: The full request body, so you can replay any request
The request id, route, status, duration and user id, but never tokens or gift codes
The bearer token, so you can tell users apart
Nothing: money services should not log

questions.q: Where must the ledger row for a money movement be written?
questions.explain: A ledger that can disagree with the balances is worse than none. Same transaction means both are saved, or neither.
options: In a log file after the response is sent
Inside the same transaction as the balance change, so the ledger can never disagree with the balances
In a queue job that runs later
In the browser's local storage

questions.q: Where does the wallet.credited event get published, and what does the e-mail job carry?
questions.explain: Exactly like order.placed in the capstone. For no lost events, write an outbox row inside the transaction instead. Jobs are stored and logged, so keep secrets out of them.
options: Inside the transaction; the job carries the gift code
After db.transaction returns; the job carries ids and amounts only, never the gift code
Before the transaction starts; the job carries the bearer token
Nowhere: e-mails are sent inside the route handler

questions.q: You count failures with a wallet.failed metric. What should its label be?
questions.explain: Labels should have few possible values and no personal or secret data. An error code tells you what is going wrong; user ids and codes belong nowhere near a metric.
options: The user id, to see who fails most
The gift code that was tried
The error code, such as ERR_CONFLICT
The full error message with the request body

questions.q: How do you check that your new tests really protect you?
questions.explain: A test that passes on broken code proves nothing. Every incident needs a test that failed on the old code and passes now.
options: Run them twice and check they pass both times
Point them at the old logic for a moment: the race test and the transfer test must fail
Delete the database and run them again
Count the number of expect calls

questions.q: The race test passes with PGlite. Why should it also run against real PostgreSQL in CI?
questions.explain: A race needs real concurrency. The fixed code is safe either way, but only a real server proves it.
options: PGlite does not support RETURNING
PGlite runs one transaction at a time, so it is gentler than production; with several real connections, transactions really run at the same time
Real PostgreSQL is needed for Promise.allSettled
Vitest cannot measure PGlite tests

questions.q: Finish isGiftCode(input). Trim the input, then return true only when it is a string that matches: GIFT- followed by 4 to 40 characters that are upper-case letters, digits or -. The program should print [ true, true, false, false, false ].
questions.explain: Check the type first: a number has no trim. The anchors ^ and $ make the whole value match, so nothing can be appended. The query still uses $1 as the second wall.

questions.q: Finish walletQuery(userId). Return { text, values } where text is exactly SELECT balance_cents FROM wallets WHERE user_id = $1 and values holds the user id. Never put the id in the text. The program should print the text and then [ '1; DROP TABLE wallets' ].
questions.explain: The hostile value sits in values, where the database treats it as data only. The SQL text is the same for every call.
questions.expected:
SELECT balance_cents FROM wallets WHERE user_id = $1
[ '1; DROP TABLE wallets' ]

questions.q: Finish redeem(cards, wallets, userId, code). Claim the card in one step: if it exists and redeemedBy is null, set redeemedBy to userId, add its amount to the user's wallet, and return 200. Otherwise change nothing and return 404. The program should print 200 404 404 and { '1': 6000, '2': 1000 }.
questions.explain: A used card and a missing card both give 404, so nobody learns which codes exist. Checking and claiming together is the JavaScript version of UPDATE … AND redeemed_by IS NULL RETURNING.

questions.q: Finish transfer(wallets, from, to, amount) so it is all or nothing. Return 400 unless amount is a whole number from 1 to 100000 and to !== from; 409 if the sender has less than amount; 404 if the receiver has no wallet. Only when all checks pass, move the money and return 200. The program should print 400 404 409 200 and { '1': 500, '2': 1500 }.
questions.explain: Validate first, then check every condition before changing anything. In the real module a database transaction gives the same guarantee, and a conditional UPDATE does the balance check.

questions.q: Finish getMyWallet(request). Find the user only from the Bearer token in request.headers.authorization (look it up in sessions), and return { status: 200, balanceCents } for that user. Ignore request.params.userId. Without a valid token return { status: 401 }. The program should print 200 1000 and 401 undefined.
questions.explain: Linus asked for user 1's wallet in the URL, but he only ever gets his own. This is the /wallets/me fix for the IDOR. (The real server looks up a hash of the token.)

questions.q: Finish can(user, action, ownerId). A customer may "read" and "move" only their own wallet (user.id === ownerId). support may "read" any wallet but may never "move" money. Return true or false. The program should print [ true, false, true, false, true ].
questions.explain: Deny by default: an unknown role gets false. Support staff help customers by reading, but moving money stays with the owner.

questions.q: Finish recordFailure(userId, now) and isLocked(userId, now). After 10 failed redemptions in a row, a user is locked for 15 minutes (LOCK_MS) from the 10th failure. Keep the count and the lock time per user in state. The program should print false true true false.
questions.explain: The time is passed in, so the result is the same on every run. After the lock ends, the user can try again; together with a per-IP limit this makes guessing codes hopeless.

questions.q: Finish transfer(from, to, amount). Work on a copy of db (both wallets and ledger): take the money from from, give it to to, and push one ledger entry { from, to, amount }. Throw new Error("No wallet") if to has no wallet. Only if nothing threw, replace db with the copy. The program should print ledger: 1 wallets: 500 1500.
questions.explain: The failed transfer changed only the copy, so neither the balances nor the ledger moved. Writing the ledger row in the same transaction is what keeps the two from ever disagreeing.

questions.q: Finish logLine(entry). Return a JSON string with only requestId, route, status and userId from entry, in that order. Everything else, such as the gift code and the token, must be left out. The program should print {"requestId":"req-9","route":"POST /giftcards/redeem","status":200,"userId":1}.
questions.explain: An allow-list is safer than a block-list: new secret fields added later are left out automatically. A gift code in a log is money anyone with log access can spend.
